overview.body:
**Bhūdevī** ​(*bhudevi*) — ‌Earth goddess ‌· seated ​on lotus ​· grain ​vessel — ​belongs to ​the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Earth, ‌Fertility, Sustenance". ​The name ‌means ​"Earth goddess; ​seated on ​a lotus, ​holding a ​vessel of ‌grain"[^1].

**Bhūdevī** ​is the ‌earth ​beneath your ‌feet made ​divine. She ‌is the ​soil that ‌feeds, the ​ground that ​bears, ‌the patient ‌mother who ‌provides without ​demand. Seated ​on a ‌lotus and ​holding a ​vessel ‌of grain, ​she is ​the agricultural ‌and ecological ​heart of ‌Hindu cosmology.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the ​name as ​**Bhūdevī** and ‌serves its ‌temple at ​[bhūdevī.com](https://xn--bhdev-q3a85b.com). The ‌restoration preserves ​at least ​one ‌distinctive feature ‌— a ‌diacritic or ‌a distinctive ​letter — ‌that the ​ASCII form ​loses, ​and exactly ‌one historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ‌the name ​in Tier ​1. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*bhudevi* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari as ​**भूदेवी**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Earth ​goddess; seated ​on a ‌lotus, holding ​a ​vessel of ‌grain"[^1].

The ​ASCII form ‌*bhudevi* survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ​system could ​not carry ​diacritics; it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Bhūdevī** ‌recovers the ​vowel length ‌of the ​original ​directly in ‌the address ‌bar. The ‌restoration preserves ​at ​least one ‌distinctive feature ​— a ​diacritic or ‌a ​distinctive letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ​form loses, ‌and exactly ​one ​historically valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, which ‌places the ‌name ​in Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**b** ‌→ **B** ‌— Bha, ‌capitalized
- ​**h** → ‌**h** ​— Ha
​- **u** ​→ **ū** ‌— Long ​ū ​(macron)
- ​**d** → ‌**d** — ​Da
- ​**e** ​→ **e** ‌— Short ​e
- ‌**v** → ​**v** — ‌Va
​- **i** ‌→ **ī** ‌— Long ​ī (macron)

​The ​canonical temple ​for this ‌name is ‌served at ​**bhūdevī.com**[^2].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/bʱuːˈdeːʋiː/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

‌- ​**Bhū-** ‌— ​Aspirated ‌labial stop ​plus ​long ​ū, ​'earth'.
​- ‌**-de-** — ​Short ‌e ​in ‌the ​divine ‌element deva.
​- ‌**-vī** ​— ​Long ‌ī, ‌the ‌feminine of ​'divine' ​— ‌the ​goddess.

​For ‌the modern ​speaker, ​the ‌closest ​approximation ‌is: ​'BHOO-day-VEE' — ​the ​first ​and ‌last ‌syllables ​are long, ‌giving ​the ​name ‌a ‌measured, ‌grounding ‌rhythm.

Kindred ​and ‌historical ​forms ​of ​the ‌name:

- ​**Sanskrit** ​— ​भूदेवी ‌(Bhūdevī), ​'Earth ​goddess'

Bhūdevī ​is ‌the ​personification ‌of ​the ‌earth ​itself as ‌a ‌goddess. ​Her ​name ​joins ​bhū ('earth') ‌with ‌devī ​('goddess').

domains.body:
**Bhūdevī** ​is ‌the ‌earth ​beneath ​your ​feet made ​divine. ​She ‌is ​the ​soil ‌that ​feeds, ‌the ​ground ‌that ​bears, ​the ​patient mother ​who ​provides ‌without ​demand. ‌Seated ​on ‌a ​lotus ‌and ​holding ‌a ​vessel of ​grain, ‌she ‌is ‌the ​agricultural ​and ‌ecological ​heart ​of ‌Hindu ​cosmology.[^1]

​### ‌Fertility

The ​power ‌of ​seed, ​sprout, ​and ​harvest ‌that ‌sustains ​all ‌life.

​### ​Sustenance

‌She provides ‌food, ‌water, ‌and ​the ‌material ​basis ​of ​existence.

‌### ​Patience

​The ​earth bears ‌the ​weight ​of ​all ‌beings ​and ‌all ​histories.

‌### ​Sacred ‌Ground

‌Every ​temple, river, ​and ​field ​participates ‌in ‌her ​body.

mythology.body:
Bhūdevī's ​myths are ‌myths of ‌rescue and ​provision. The ​earth is ​not ​inert matter; ​she is ‌a goddess ​who can ​be stolen, ‌rescued, ​and petitioned.[^1]

‌### Varāha ​Lifts the ‌Earth (Rescue)

​When the ​demon ​Hiraṇyākṣa casts ​the earth ​into the ‌cosmic ocean, ​Viṣṇu ‌descends as ​Varāha, the ‌boar avatar. ​He dives ‌into the ​waters, ‌lifts Bhūdevī ​on his ​tusk, and ‌restores her ‌to her ‌place ​in the ​cosmos. She ‌becomes his ​consort in ​this rescue ‌myth.[^2]

​### The ​Birth of ‌Sītā (Birth)

​In the ‌Rāmāyaṇa, Sītā ​is ​discovered in ​a furrow ​of the ‌earth by ‌King Janaka. ​The ‌furrow (*sītā*) ​identifies her ​as a ‌daughter of ‌Bhūdevī, linking ‌the ‌earth goddess ​to the ‌ideal of ​wifely devotion ​and patient ​endurance.

‌### Earth ​as Altar ​(Cult)

In ​Vedic and ‌later ​Hindu ritual, ​the ground ​itself is ‌sacred. Before ​any sacrifice ‌or ​temple construction, ‌the earth ​is propitiated. ‌Bhūdevī makes ‌explicit what ​the ​ritual already ​assumes: the ​land is ‌a goddess, ‌not a ​possession.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Bhūdevī ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Sanskrit ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming भूदेवी, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to earth ​and ‌iconography ​matching ​its ​traditional ‌attributes ​(lotus and ​grain ​vessel). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sources.citation: Srinivasan, Many Heads, Arms, and Eyes.

meditation.body:
Bhūdevī ​is ‌the ‌quietest ​of the ​great ​goddesses. ​She ​does ‌not ​brandish ​weapons ‌or ride ​into ‌battle; ​she ‌simply ​holds ​everything. ​Every ​footstep is ​a ‌pressure ​on ‌her ​body; ‌every ​harvest ‌is a ​gift ‌from ​her ​substance. ‌She ‌is ‌the ​ground of ​being ‌made ​literal.

​To ‌worship ​Bhūdevī ​is ‌to refuse ​the ‌modern ​fantasy ​that ​the ​earth ‌is ‌dead resource. ​The ‌soil ​is ​alive, ‌aware, ‌and ‌patient ‌beyond human ​measure. ‌The ​grain ​vessel ​in ‌her ​hand ​is not ​a ‌symbol ​of ​wealth ​but ‌of ​dependence: ‌we eat ​the ‌earth, ​and ‌the ‌earth ​permits ​it. ​That permission ​is ‌a ‌sacred ​trust.[^1]
